title: Contrastive Order Learning: A General Framework for Ordinal Regression
claim: Prior contrastive methods use hard, binary or partial positive/negative assignments; ours compares all samples with soft, rank-aware weights.
layout: 3 panels side-by-side, left-to-right, shared rank axis with colored links
description: Three rounded gray panels sit side by side, labeled (a) SupCon, (b) RnC and (c) ConOrd. Each shows an anchor face photo (age 24) at left and a horizontal rank axis with dots. Face photos with age labels (14, 18, 24, 27, 32, 60, 75) sit above and below the axis. Lines connect each face to its dot on the axis. In SupCon, only one sample is blue (positive) and every other sample is red (negative). In RnC, some samples are blue or red and the rest are faded gray, marked as neglected. In ConOrd, every sample gets a smooth blue-to-white-to-red gradient according to its rank distance from the anchor. The legends at the top of each panel explain the colors. The eye goes first to the color shift from hard red/blue and gray blocks to soft gradients in the rightmost panel.
caption: Comparison of three contrastive learning techniques: (a) supervised contrastive learning (SupCon) [ref], (b) Rank-N-Contrast (RnC) [ref], and (c) the proposed ConOrd. SupCon considers the augmented view of an anchor as the only positive and treats all the others as negatives. RnC selects one sample as a positive and defines negatives as those with rank differences greater than the anchor–positive pair. Different from these existing techniques, ConOrd compares all samples in a batch by defining positive and negative samples in a soft manner.
abstract: We propose contrastive order learning (ConOrd), a contrastive learning framework for ordinal regression that integrates the strengths of contrastive learning and order learning. While contrastive learning effectively leverages all samples in a batch, it typically ignores the inherent ordering among rank labels. Conversely, order learning explicitly models label ordinality but often relies on local, margin-based comparisons, limiting its ability to capture global ordinal structure. ConOrd addresses these limitations by introducing a contrastive order loss with soft affinity and disparity weights based on rank differences, enabling fine-grained modeling of ordinal relationships across all sample pairs within a batch. Extensive experiments on a range of ordinal regression tasks, including facial age estimation, blind image quality assessment, and blind video quality assessment, demonstrate that ConOrd consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance and generalizes well across diverse ordinal regression scenarios. The source code is available at https://github.com/cwlee00/ConOrd.
